title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered, paired confirmatory study that measured whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—LLM initial generation (shared initial candidate) + deterministic network verifier (Batfish-style validator) + an automated, single-step LLM repair—reduces verifier-detected semantic/safety failures for intent→vendor‑CLI NetOps tasks. We executed the frozen preregistration (study cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) using gpt-5-mini on a 300‑intent task set (two vendor dialect clusters). After infrastructure exclusions 266 paired units completed. Baseline (initial candidate) verifier pass: 260/266 (97.74%). Final guarded (GVR) verifier pass: 265/266 (99.62%). Paired difference = 0.01880 (1.88 percentage points); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00376, 0.03759]. Repair-stage activity was rare (6 repair calls recorded). Under the preregistered analysis rules the observed improvement did not meet the α=0.05 threshold for the primary confirmatory test. We present the experimental design, deterministic validation criteria, primary and sensitivity analyses, and a focused discussion of operational implications and validity threats. All claims are traceable to the archived preregistration, execution manifest, and analysis artifacts produced during the autonomous run.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and zero‑touch configuration generation [10.1145/3656296; 10.1109/comst.2025.3526606]. Their stochastic generation, however, risks producing syntactic or semantic violations (‘‘hallucinations’’) that can cause outages or unsafe network states, motivating grounded pipelines that interpose deterministic verifiers and bounded repair loops [10.2139/ssrn.6754899]. We ask: does a preregistered GVR pipeline that uses an LLM for initial generation, a deterministic network validator (Batfish‑style), and a single automated repair step reduce verifier‑detected failures relative to the initial LLM candidate? Our contribution is an artifact‑grounded, preregistered paired experiment and its autonomous execution and analysis (study id cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1), together with an evidence‑backed interpretation of practical implications and threats to validity.
sections.related_work: Prior work documents active interest in LLMs for network configuration and intent‑based NetOps, including benchmarks and prototype systems that translate natural intent into device CLI or API calls [10.1145/3656296; 10.1109/comst.2025.3526606]. The generate–verify–repair (GVR) idea—placing deterministic validators between stochastic generation and acceptance—has been proposed to reconcile probabilistic generation with deterministic correctness requirements in regulated settings [10.2139/ssrn.6754899]. Network verification tools (Batfish and related header‑space and real‑time checkers) are standard validator candidates for NetOps pipelines and have been proposed as verification oracles in LLM‑augmented workflows [10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Surveys of LLM failure modes and grounding strategies emphasize RAG, tool augmentation, and constrained decoding as mitigation directions but note sparse production‑scale evidence in NetOps contexts [10.1109/comst.2025.3526606; 10.2139/ssrn.6116106]. Our study directly evaluates GVR with a deterministic NetOps validator on a preregistered task corpus.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study plan (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) fixed a paired estimand: the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, a two‑condition shared_initial_candidate design, and N=300 planned intent pairs drawn from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a deterministic synthetic task generator. The model and orchestration were fixed in the preregistration (gpt-5-mini; adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1). Execution contract: each task produced exactly one initial LLM generation (shared initial candidate). If the deterministic validator rejected that candidate, the allowed guarded pipeline could invoke at most one automated repair call (single repair attempt per preregistered retry policy). Deterministic verification: we used a Batfish‑style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) that performs structural and reachability checks and returns categorical pass/fail with violation codes. Inclusion/exclusion and missingness: infrastructure/API failures triggered the preregistered retry policy (up to two automatic retries) and deterministic exclusion rules; pairs with irrecoverable infrastructure failures were handled per preregistered missingness plan and sensitivity analyses. Execution artifacts: the autonomous run produced raw model outputs, validator traces, provider call logs, and a reproducible execution manifest; the run completed under the preregistered adapter and manifest (planned 600 episodes; completed 532 episodes; 266 complete pairs after exclusions). All code, prompts, and manifests are archived with hashes as reported in the execution manifest.
sections.results: Primary confirmatory outcome: of 266 completed paired units, baseline initial candidates passed deterministic validation in 260 cases (97.744%), and the final guarded (GVR) outcome passed in 265 cases (99.624%). Contingency counts (guarded,baseline): n11=260, n10=5 (guarded pass, baseline fail), n01=0 (guarded fail, baseline pass), n00=1. Paired difference estimate = 0.018796992481203034. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. Paired bootstrap (B=10,000, seed 1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0037594, 0.03759398]. Under the preregistered two‑sided α=0.05 decision rule the McNemar test did not reach statistical significance. Operational diagnostics: repair activity was rare—the provider_call_audit records 6 repair calls across the run (stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=300, repair=6), indicating most initial candidates already satisfied validator constraints. Missingness and infrastructure: 34 episodes failed due to infrastructure/model‑call errors and were treated per preregistered rules (complete_pair_primary exclusion); sensitivity analyses (treating failed calls as failures) are recorded in the archived artifacts. No planned secondary hypothesis test passed multiplicity thresholds; secondary descriptive artifacts (latency, repair iteration distributions) are archived for inspection.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The GVR pipeline produced a small absolute increase in verifier pass rate (~1.9 percentage points). The paired test p=0.0625 narrowly missed α=0.05; the bootstrap CI lies entirely above zero under the chosen bootstrap procedure, illustrating the dependence of inferential conclusions on test choice and the low discordant pair count (n10=5). Practically, the recorded low repair frequency (6 repair calls) implies that for the chosen task set and LLM, initial candidates were already highly likely to satisfy the deterministic validator, limiting room for the guarded pipeline to improve outcomes. Operational implications: in settings where initial LLM outputs are already high‑quality for the target validator, a GVR pipeline can add deterministic assurance at modest repair invocation rates; however, the marginal benefit may be small. Construct and external validity: our tasks were intent→CLI scenarios (two synthetic vendor dialect clusters) with deterministic topologies and a Batfish‑style validator; results do not imply universal GVR benefit across all vendor languages, larger topologies, or production‑scale heterogeneity. Methodological note on shared_initial_candidate: under the executed semantics both baseline and guarded conditions began from the same initial generation; any paired difference arises only from the validator‑triggered guarded repair step, consistent with the preregistration.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired study testing whether a GVR pipeline using an LLM (gpt-5-mini) plus a deterministic Batfish‑style validator and a single automated repair step reduces verifier‑detected failures for intent→CLI NetOps tasks. Across 266 completed pairs the guarded pipeline yielded a small absolute increase in final verifier pass rate (1.88 percentage points); this improvement did not meet the preregistered α=0.05 threshold in the exact McNemar test (p=0.0625). Repair invocations were rare, suggesting limited headroom for improvement on this task set and model. The results support cautious operational consideration of validator‑centric pipelines as low‑overhead assurance mechanisms, while highlighting the need for broader evaluations across vendor dialects, larger topologies, and higher baseline failure regimes. All artifacts, raw outputs, validator traces, and the preregistration are archived for reproducibility and further exploratory analysis.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an explicit autonomy lock. Models and tools: hosted LLM gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version gpt-5-mini) was used for generation; the orchestration adapter was the preregistered hosted_netops_gvr_v1 pipeline; deterministic validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (Batfish‑style checks). The initial master prompt for the autonomous run is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The experimental plan was preregistered (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1; preregistration manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891) and frozen before execution. Human role: before the autonomy lock a human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) and approved pre‑lock infrastructure development; after the lock no human edited or rewrote technical content, prompts, outputs, analyses, or manuscript text. The autonomous pipeline performed literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, verification, analysis, autonomous peer review, revision, and manuscript generation. Tools and allowed capabilities are recorded in the archived execution manifest. No undisclosed human manuscript editing occurred post‑lock; all execution and analysis artifacts are archived with recorded hashes (execution artifact manifest referenced in the paper).
limitations: Confirmatory sample: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure exclusions 266 pairs completed; 34 episodes were lost to API/infrastructure failures and excluded as preregistered—this reduces effective sample size and inference precision.

Design scope: tasks were intent→CLI scenarios drawn from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a deterministic synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; external validity to other vendors, larger topologies, or production traffic is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both baseline and guarded conditions began from the same initial candidate; the guarded effect is strictly the validator‑triggered repair; the study does not measure alternative constrained‑prompting strategies that would produce independent initial candidates.
Validator coverage: deterministic validator checks (Batfish‑style) have finite coverage; undetected semantic violations outside validator checks are possible and not measured here.
Low repair activity: only six repair calls occurred, limiting statistical power to evaluate properties of the repair loop (convergence, typical repair content) in diverse failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the exact McNemar test yielded p=0.0625 while a bootstrap CI for the paired difference was entirely positive under the chosen bootstrap procedure; interpretive conclusions depend on the chosen inferential method and the small discordant‑pair counts.
